title: STRANGE MINUTE #16 · WHAT IF

lines.text: What if every ocean turned into fresh water?
Right now, every liter of seawater holds about 35 grams of salt.
lines.say: Right now, every liter of seawater holds about thirty-five grams of salt.

lines.text: Spread all that salt on land, and it'd be over 500 feet thick.
lines.say: Spread all that salt on land, and it'd be over five hundred feet thick.

lines.text: Good news: you could drink straight from the ocean.
Bad news: almost all sea life is built for salt.
Water floods into their cells, and most can't survive.
Coral reefs would die. So would most sea fish.
Fresh water also freezes sooner: at 32 degrees, not 28.
lines.say: Fresh water also freezes sooner: at thirty-two degrees, not twenty-eight.

lines.text: Polar seas would ice over much faster.
And the giant currents that carry heat around the planet?
They run partly on salt. They'd slow down.
Places like Europe could get a lot colder.
So, would you trade the salt for a drinkable ocean?

sources: NOAA: average ocean salinity ~35 ppt (~35 g/L); NOAA: if ocean salt were spread over land it would form a layer >500 ft (152 m) thick
Seawater freezes ~28.4 °F (−1.9 °C) vs 32 °F; osmotic stress kills most marine organisms in fresh water; AMOC is driven by temperature+salinity (thermohaline) — weakening would cool Europe
